source.title_on_document: Neural Mechanisms of Collaborative Creative Thinking in Engineering Design: Human-Human Versus Human-AI Interaction

supplement.where: The paper refers to no supplementary material or online appendix.

paper_design_summary: Fourteen male engineering students in a within-subject EEG experiment each did an engineering design (divergent thinking) task under three conditions: alone, with another human, and with GPT-4; the order of conditions was counterbalanced between subjects. Two creativity researchers rated each idea on 5-point originality and usefulness scales, and conditions were compared with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Most of the paper reports EEG source activity (eLORETA) during the idea-thinking phase.

studies.label: Within-subject EEG experiment (engineering design ideation: individual vs human-human vs human-AI)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Order of the three conditions (individual, human-human, human-AI); every participant did all three. The paper says the order was counterbalanced, not that it was randomized.
assignment.quote: All experimental participants performed the following three conditions. The order of implementation of the conditions was counterbalanced between subjects.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 3 (printed p. 330), Section 2.3; also PDF p. 5 (printed p. 332), Section 2.4 ('within-subject design')

arms.name: Individual
arms.description: Engineering design task requiring divergent thinking performed by a single individual on their own; in the idea recognition phase the participant reads their own idea.

arms.name: Human-Human
arms.description: Two persons performed the engineering task; in the idea recognition phase the participant reads the partner's idea.

arms.name: Human-AI
arms.description: An individual performed the engineering task with the help of AI (GPT-4); in the idea recognition phase the participant reads the AI's idea.

participants.exclusions: None reported. Fourteen participants are described in Methods and Figure 2 reports scores for the 14 participants. Every participant did all three conditions, so 14 people contribute to every arm.
participants.who: Male engineering students, healthy, all right-handed; two participants took part in each experimental session
participants.country: not_stated (University of Tokyo ethics approval and author affiliation suggest Japan)
participants.quote: Fourteen male students of engineering participated in this study. All students were healthy with no brain-related diseases or disabilities; two participants participated in each experiment.
participants.locator: PDF p. 3 (printed p. 330), Section 2.1; PDF p. 5 (printed p. 332), Section 3

ai_tool.how_used: In the human-AI condition an individual performed the task 'with the help of AI (GPT-4)'. Each round had a 30 s thinking phase, a 30 s typing phase, and a 10 s idea recognition phase in which the participant read the AI's idea. The paper does not describe how the AI ideas were produced or whether participants could prompt GPT-4 freely; the role code is a best fit.

task.description: Open-ended engineering design task requiring divergent thinking (from Hay et al. 2019): propose original product solutions to societal problems, e.g., designing a product to reduce the space needed to store glass products at home before recycling. Per problem: problem recognition, then 10 repetitions of divergent thinking (30 s), idea output (30 s, typing), idea recognition (10 s).
task.duration: Each idea cycle 70 s (30 s thinking, 30 s typing, 10 s reading), repeated 10 times per problem; whole session including EEG setup within two hours. Number of problems per condition not stated.

outcomes.name: Usefulness of ideas
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two creativity researchers rated each idea on a 5-point usefulness scale ('how useful the idea is to society as a whole'). Conditions compared with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests across the 14 participants. How ratings were aggregated across raters and ideas is not stated.

contrasts.reported: Wilcoxon signed-rank test: 'the usefulness score was higher in the Human-AI condition than in the individual condition (p = 0.023)'. Fig. 2 shows mean usefulness bars (with error bars) of roughly 2.7 (Individual) and 2.9 (Human-AI) on a 1-5 scale; no numeric means, SDs, or test statistics printed.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 332), Section 3; PDF p. 6 (printed p. 333), Fig. 2

contrasts.reported: No test reported for Human-AI vs Human-Human on usefulness. Fig. 2 bars are similar (roughly 2.9 vs 2.95) with no significance marker. Text: 'the usefulness scores were higher in the human-human and human-AI conditions compared to the individual condition.'
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 332), Section 3; PDF p. 6 (printed p. 333), Fig. 2

outcomes.name: Originality of ideas
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two creativity researchers rated each idea on a 5-point originality scale (1 'not original at all' to 5 'very original'). Wilcoxon signed-rank tests across the 14 participants. Aggregation across raters and ideas not stated.

contrasts.reported: 'The originality scores did not differ between conditions.' No p-value printed. Fig. 2 bars roughly 2.6 (Individual) and 2.55 (Human-AI) on a 1-5 scale.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 332), Section 3; PDF p. 6 (printed p. 333), Fig. 2

contrasts.reported: 'The originality scores did not differ between conditions.' No p-value printed. Fig. 2 bars roughly 2.6 (Human-Human) and 2.55 (Human-AI).
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 332), Section 3; PDF p. 6 (printed p. 333), Fig. 2

company_involvement.description: Conducted as part of a collaborative research project with Ricoh Company, Ltd.; co-author Yukihisa Yokoyama is a Ricoh employee. Ricoh is not the AI provider (the AI is GPT-4).
company_involvement.locator: PDF p. 1 (printed p. 328), author affiliations; PDF p. 8 (printed p. 335), Disclosure of Interests

eligibility.reason: Within-subject experiment in which each participant worked alone, with a human partner, and with GPT-4; the order was counterbalanced, but the paper does not say it was randomized (criterion 1 unclear). Only 14 participants (criterion 2 not met, far below 50). Ideas were rated by two creativity researchers for originality and usefulness (criterion 3 met). Belongs in the screening report as a small experiment, not in the dataset.

one_line_finding: With 14 engineering students, ideas produced with GPT-4 were rated more useful than ideas produced alone (Wilcoxon p = 0.023), while originality did not differ across conditions (p. 332, Section 3; Fig. 2, p. 333).
open_questions: Whether counterbalanced condition order counts as randomized order for criterion 1 (moot here because N = 14).
How participants interacted with GPT-4 is not described: the AI's idea is read in the 10 s recognition phase, but whether participants prompted it is not stated.
Whether the Wilcoxon tests use participant-level mean scores is implied by the signed-rank design but not stated.
notes: Printed pages 328-336 correspond to PDF pages 1-9. The paper's main focus is EEG source activity (Fig. 3, p. 334), which is not a creativity outcome scored on output and is not listed. Fig. 2 values are approximate readings of bar heights; no numeric means are printed. The usefulness scale labels as printed contain an apparent typo ('4. very much so,' '3. very much so').
